title: Integrating rational functions by partial fractions
pattern: Write a proper rational function as a sum over the factors of its denominator, then integrate each term.
applies: The integrand is rational and the domain excludes denominator zeros.
steps: Use polynomial division if the numerator degree is at least the denominator degree.
Factor the remaining denominator and set up a term for every required factor power.
Clear denominators, solve the coefficient equations, and integrate the decomposition.
pitfalls: Repeated factors need a term for each power. An irreducible quadratic uses a linear numerator.
Integrals of 1/(x−a) use ln|x−a| on each domain interval.
checks: Recombine the fractions and differentiate the antiderivative.

example.answer: 2 ln|x−1|+3 ln|x+2|+C on each interval avoiding −2 and 1.

title: Trigonometric substitution
pattern: Use x=a sin θ for √(a²−x²), x=a tan θ for √(a²+x²), or x=a sec θ for √(x²−a²).
applies: A radical matches one of the standard forms with a>0. Choose a branch compatible with the integration interval.
steps: Select the trigonometric substitution and compute dx.
Use a trigonometric identity to simplify the radical with the correct sign.
Integrate in θ and convert back to x or use transformed definite bounds.
pitfalls: Track absolute values when taking a square root of a square.
Keep the inverse-trigonometric branch consistent with the substitution interval.
checks: Differentiate the final expression on the stated domain.

title: Volume of revolution by washers
pattern: Slices perpendicular to the axis give V=π∫(R²−r²) ds.
applies: The solid comes from revolving a planar region about a line. Each chosen slice forms a disk or annulus.
steps: Choose the slicing variable perpendicular to the axis.
Express the outer and inner radii as distances from the axis.
Integrate the cross-sectional area over the slice interval.
pitfalls: Use the difference of squared radii.
If the axis crosses a slice, check whether the inner radius becomes zero.
checks: Verify R≥r≥0 on each integration interval.

example.problem: Rotate 1≤y≤3−x, 0≤x≤2 about the x-axis. Find the volume.

title: Volume of revolution by cylindrical shells
pattern: Slices parallel to the axis give V=2π∫ radius·height ds.
applies: The region is described by shell heights at each radius, with each shell counted once.
steps: Choose slices parallel to the axis and let the integration variable measure their positions.
Write the radius as the distance to the axis and the height as the slice length.
Integrate circumference times height over the radial range.
pitfalls: For a shifted axis, use the distance to that axis.
Slices on both sides of the axis can sweep the same shell. Combine their contributions geometrically.
checks: Check that the height and radius are nonnegative and use consistent bounds.

example.problem: Rotate the region 0≤y≤x(2−x), 0≤x≤2 about the y-axis. Find the volume.

title: Product and quotient rules
applies: The component functions are differentiable and a quotient denominator is nonzero.
steps: Identify the outer product or quotient.
Differentiate each component using any needed chain or product rules.
Combine the terms and evaluate at the requested point.
pitfalls: The quotient numerator starts with u′v.
A product derivative has two terms even if one vanishes at the evaluation point.
checks: For a quotient, keep the original denominator squared.

title: Ratio test for series
pattern: Let L=lim |a_(n+1)/a_n|. If L<1 the series converges absolutely, and if L>1 it diverges.
applies: Terms are nonzero eventually and the ratio limit exists or is infinite.
steps: Form the absolute ratio of successive terms.
Simplify it before taking the limit.
Compare with one and switch tests if the result is one.
pitfalls: A limit of one is inconclusive.
Use the absolute ratio for signed terms.
checks: Look for cancellation of factorials or powers before evaluating the limit.

example.problem: Decide whether Σ from n=1 to ∞ of n²(−3/5)^n converges absolutely.
example.answer: It converges absolutely. The ratio limit is 3/5.

title: Direct and limit comparison for series
pattern: For nonnegative terms, use eventual inequalities or a finite positive limit of a_n/b_n.
applies: The terms of both series are nonnegative eventually. For limit comparison, b_n must be positive eventually.
steps: Choose a familiar benchmark series with similar term size.
Prove the needed eventual inequality or take the limit of the term ratio.
Transfer convergence or divergence using the correct comparison direction.
pitfalls: For direct comparison, an upper convergent bound proves convergence and a lower divergent bound proves divergence.
A finite positive ratio makes the two series share convergence behavior.
checks: Identify the benchmark and show the comparison explicitly.

example.problem: Decide whether Σ from n=1 to ∞ of (2n+1)/(n³+4) converges.
example.answer: It converges by limit comparison with Σ 1/n². The term ratio tends to 2.

title: Change of variables with a Jacobian determinant
pattern: For x=T(u), replace the volume element by |det DT(u)| du.
applies: The transformation is continuously differentiable and one-to-one on the integration interior, with nonzero Jacobian there.
steps: Choose coordinates that simplify the region or integrand.
Solve for the original variables and compute the absolute determinant of that inverse-coordinate map.
Transform the integrand and bounds and include the determinant factor.
pitfalls: Use the determinant for the map from the new variables to the original ones.
Take the absolute value and account for any overlapping coverage.
checks: A constant linear transformation scales area or volume by the absolute determinant.

title: Stokes’ theorem
pattern: ∮_C F·dr=∬_S (∇×F)·n dS, with matching boundary and surface orientations.
applies: F has continuous first partials near the oriented piecewise smooth surface, and C is its oriented boundary.
steps: Use the right-hand rule to match the boundary direction to the normal.
Compute curl F if taking the surface-integral route.
Use a simpler admissible surface with the same boundary and compatible orientation if helpful.
pitfalls: Reversing the orientation reverses the answer.
A replacement surface must stay where the vector field is smooth.
checks: Check the boundary orientation before swapping surfaces.

example.problem: Find the outward-oriented curl flux of F=(−y,x,0) through the upper hemisphere of radius 2.

title: Divergence theorem
pattern: For outward orientation, ∬_(∂V) F·n dS=∭_V ∇·F dV.
applies: The surface is the closed boundary of a solid. F has continuous first partials on a neighborhood of the solid.
steps: Identify the enclosed solid and check the outward orientation.
Compute the scalar divergence.
Integrate the divergence over the volume.
pitfalls: An open surface must be closed and the extra cap flux accounted for before using the theorem.
Check for singularities inside the volume.
checks: For constant divergence, multiply it by the enclosed volume.

example.problem: Find the outward flux of F=(x,2y,3z) through the sphere x²+y²+z²=4.
